'''Robert Allan Weinberg''' (born November 11, 1942) is an American biologist, [[Daniel K. Ludwig]] Professor for Cancer Research at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)]], director of the [[Ludwig Cancer Research|Ludwig Center]] of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], and [[American Cancer Society]] Research Professor. His research is in the area of [[oncogenes]] and the genetic basis of human cancer.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(82)90100-3| title = Isolation of a transforming sequence from a human bladder carcinoma cell line| journal = Cell| volume = 29| pages = 161–9| year = 1982| last1 = Shih | first1 = C. | last2 = Weinberg | first2 = R. A. | pmid=6286138 | issue=1| s2cid = 12046552}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/22780| pmid = 10440377| year = 1999| last1 = Weinberg | first1 = R. A. | title = Creation of human tumour cells with defined genetic elements| journal = Nature| volume = 400| issue = 6743| pages = 464–8| last2 = Hahn | first2 = W. C. | last3 = Counter | first3 = C. M. | last4 = Lundberg | first4 = A. S. | last5 = Beijersbergen | first5 = R. L. | last6 = Brooks | first6 = M. W. | bibcode = 1999Natur.400..464H| s2cid = 2377425}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2008.03.027| title = The Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition Generates Cells with Properties of Stem Cells| journal = Cell| volume = 133| issue = 4| pages = 704–15| year = 2008| last1 = Mani | first1 = S. A. | last2 = Guo | first2 = W. | last3 = Liao | first3 = M. J. | last4 = Eaton | first4 = E. N. | last5 = Ayyanan | first5 = A. | last6 = Zhou | first6 = A. Y. | last7 = Brooks | first7 = M. | last8 = Reinhard | first8 = F. | last9 = Zhang | first9 = C. C. | last10 = Shipitsin | first10 = M. | last11 = Campbell | first11 = L. L. | last12 = Polyak | first12 = K. | last13 = Brisken | first13 = C. | last14 = Yang | first14 = J. | last15 = Weinberg | first15 = R. A. | pmid=18485877 | pmc=2728032}}</ref>

Robert Weinberg is also affiliated with the [[Broad Institute]] and is a founding member of the [[Whitehead Institute]] for Biomedical Research.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dfhcc.harvard.edu/events/detail/event/the-deadly-side-of-cancer-how-cancer-spreads-with-robert-weinberg-1/|title=The Deadly Side of Cancer: How Cancer Spreads with Robert Weinberg – DF/HCC|website=www.dfhcc.harvard.edu|access-date=January 24, 2020|archive-date=December 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211215115637/https://www.dfhcc.harvard.edu/events/detail/event/the-deadly-side-of-cancer-how-cancer-spreads-with-robert-weinberg-1/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Weinberg and [[Eric Lander]], a colleague at M.I.T., are co-founders of [[Verastem Oncology|Verastem]], a biopharmaceutical company focused on discovering and developing drugs to treat cancer by targeting [[cancer stem cells]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://phx.corporate-ir.net/phoenix.zhtml?c=250749&p=irol-newsArticle&ID=1650861&highlight= |title=News Release - Novel Drugs Targeting Cancer Stem Cells |website=phx.corporate-ir.net |access-date=6 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160107075557/http://phx.corporate-ir.net/phoenix.zhtml?c=250749&p=irol-newsArticle&ID=1650861&highlight= |archive-date=7 January 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Career ==
Weinberg earned a [[B.S.]] in biology from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1964 and PhD in biology from the same institute in 1969. He was an instructor in biology at [[Stillman College]] in [[Tuscaloosa, Alabama]] (1965–1966), and a postdoc in Ernest Winocour's lab at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] (1969–1970) and in [[Renato Dulbecco]]'s lab at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] (1970–1972). He joined MIT in 1972.<ref>{{cite web |title=CV (Robert A. Weinberg) |url=https://www.psl.eu/sites/default/files/PDF/WEINBERG%20CV%202018%203.pdf |publisher=Paris Sciences et Lettres University |access-date=15 September 2020}}</ref>

== Research ==

He is best known for his discoveries of the first human [[oncogene]] [[Ras (protein)|Ras]] and the first [[tumor suppressor gene]] [[Retinoblastoma protein|Rb]]<ref name = "Emperor">{{cite book
|title=The Emperor of All Maladies: A Biography of Cancer
|author=Siddhartha Mukherjee
|isbn=978-1-4391-0795-9
|oclc=464593321
|year=2010
|publisher=Simon & Schuster
|url-access=registration
|url=https://archive.org/details/emperorofallmala00mukh
}}</ref><sup>p.&nbsp;371-381</sup>, which is partially documented in [[Natalie Angier]]′s book, [[Natural Obsessions]], about her year spent in Weinberg's lab.

In the late 20th century, advances in genetics led to the discovery of over one hundred cancer cell types. Cancer cells were noted for their bewildering diversity. It was hard to identify the principles that cancers had in common.

He and [[Douglas Hanahan]] wrote the seminal paper "[[Hallmarks of cancer|The Hallmarks of Cancer]]", published in January 2000,<ref name=Cell>{{cite journal |title=The Hallmarks of Cancer
|journal=Cell |issn=0092-8674
|volume=100 |issue=1 |pages=57–70
|author1=Hanahan, Douglas |author2=Weinberg, RA
|date=January 7, 2000
|doi=10.1016/S0092-8674(00)81683-9 |pmid=10647931|s2cid=1478778 |doi-access=free }}</ref> that gave the six requirements for one renegade cell to cause a deadly cancer:<ref name="Emperor"/> In 2011, they published an updated review article entitled "Hallmarks of cancer: the next generation".<ref>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.013
| pmid = 21376230
| last1 = Hanahan | first1 = D.
| last2 = Weinberg | first2 = R. A.
| title = Hallmarks of Cancer: The Next Generation
| journal = Cell
| volume = 144
| issue = 5
| pages = 646–674
| year = 2011
| doi-access = free
}}</ref>

Weinberg is well known for both his cancer research<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/300143a0| pmid = 6290897| title = Mechanism of activation of a human oncogene| journal = Nature| volume = 300| issue = 5888| pages = 143–9| year = 1982| last1 = Tabin | first1 = C. J. | author-link1 = Clifford Tabin| last2 = Bradley | first2 = S. M. | last3 = Bargmann | first3 = C. I. | last4 = Weinberg | first4 = R. A. | last5 = Papageorge | first5 = A. G. | last6 = Scolnick | first6 = E. M. | last7 = Dhar | first7 = R. | last8 = Lowy | first8 = D. R. | last9 = Chang | first9 = E. H.
| bibcode = 1982Natur.300..143T| s2cid = 4253259}}</ref> and for his mentorship of many eminent scientists, including [[Tyler Jacks]], [https://www.dfhcc.harvard.edu/insider/member-detail/member/william-c-hahn-md-phd/ William C. Hahn], [[Clifford Tabin]], [[Sendurai Mani]] and [[Cornelia Bargmann]]. He is currently studying cancer cell metastasis.<ref>{{cite journal |journal=Science |date=March 25, 2011 |pages=1559–1564 |volume=331 |title=A perspective on Cancer Cell Metastasis |author1=Christine L. Chaffer |author2=Robert A. Weinberg |issue=6024 |doi=10.1126/science.1203543 |pmid=21436443 |df=mdy-all |bibcode=2011Sci...331.1559C |s2cid=10550070 }}</ref>

He is also the author of the textbook ''The Biology of Cancer''<ref name=boc>{{cite book
  | last = Weinberg
  | first = Robert
  | title = The Biology of Cancer
  | publisher = Garland Science
  | isbn = 978-0-8153-4076-8
  | oclc=63114199
  | year = 2007
  | publication-date = 2006 }}</ref> published by [[Garland Science]], as well as two important accounts intended for a wider audience: ''One Renegade Cell: How Cancer Begins'' (1999) (Science Masters Series); and ''Racing to the Beginning of the Road: The Search for the Origin of Cancer'' (1996).

{{As of|2026}}, Weinberg has an [[h-index]] of 222 according to [[Google Scholar]].<ref>{{Google Scholar id}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
In 1985, Weinberg received the [[Academy of Achievement|Golden Plate Award]] of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> Weinberg won the [[National Medal of Science]] and the [[Keio Medical Science Prize]] in 1997. In 1999, he received the [[Albert Einstein World Award of Science]] in recognition of his valuable and pioneering contributions in the field of Biomedical Sciences and for his productive trajectory related to the genetic and molecular basis of neoplastic disease.<ref>{{cite web|title=Albert Einstein World Award of Science 1999|url=http://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/winners-science-robertweinberg.php|access-date=August 13, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140304223356/http://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/winners-science-robertweinberg.php|archive-date=March 4, 2014|df=mdy-all}}</ref> He was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Robert+A.+Weinberg&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-07-15|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> He obtained the [[Wolf Prize in Medicine]] in 2004 (shared with [[Roger Y. Tsien]]), and he is a member of the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]]. In 2007 he received an honorary doctorate degree in commemoration of [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] from [[Uppsala University]]. He is a member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] since 1992.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kva.se/en/Members/Ledamoter-page/?personId=679|title=The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences: Robert Weinberg|access-date=2009-09-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403051257/https://www.kva.se/en/Members/Ledamoter-page/?personId=679|archive-date=April 3, 2019|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}</ref> In 2009 he was presented the Hope Funds Award in Basic Research.<ref>{{cite web |title=2009 Honorees |url=http://www.hope-funds.org/honorees/2009-honorees/ |website=hope-funds.org |date=January 2, 2009 |access-date=15 September 2020}}</ref> In 2013 he was awarded the $3 million [[Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences]] for his work <ref>{{cite web |title=LAUREATES 2013 |publisher=Breakthrough Prize in Lifesciences |url=https://breakthroughprizeinlifesciences.org/laureates2 |access-date=December 19, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219203903/https://breakthroughprizeinlifesciences.org/laureates2 |archive-date=December 19, 2013 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> and in 2021 he received the [[Japan Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.japanprize.jp/|title=The Japan Prize Foundation|website=The Japan Prize Foundation}}</ref>

== Retractions ==
To this day Weinberg has had five research papers retracted where he is listed as a co-author. The retractions include one paper in Cell, one in Cancer Cell, two in Genes & Development and one in Cancer Research.<ref>{{cite web|title = Papers from MIT Cancer Biologist's Laboratory Retracted|website = [[The Boston Globe]]|url = https://www.bostonglobe.com/news/science/2015/03/19/papers-from-mit-cancer-biologist-laboratory-retracted/7NABAzMU2BMLxb9b67wMrK/story.html|url-status = live|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150729024738/https://www.bostonglobe.com/news/science/2015/03/19/papers-from-mit-cancer-biologist-laboratory-retracted/7NABAzMU2BMLxb9b67wMrK/story.html|archive-date = July 29, 2015|df = mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title = Three Retractions for Highly Cited Author|url = http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/42503/title/Three-Retractions-for-Highly-Cited-Author/|url-status = live|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150523193322/http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view%2FarticleNo%2F42503%2Ftitle%2FThree-Retractions-for-Highly-Cited-Author%2F|archive-date = May 23, 2015|df = mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title = Cancer Research retraction is fifth for Robert Weinberg, fourth for his former student|url = http://retractionwatch.com/2015/07/06/cancer-research-retraction-is-fifth-for-robert-weinberg-fourth-for-his-former-student/|url-status = live|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150910084748/http://retractionwatch.com/2015/07/06/cancer-research-retraction-is-fifth-for-robert-weinberg-fourth-for-his-former-student/|archive-date = September 10, 2015|df = mdy-all|date = July 6, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title = Retraction of Cell paper by Robert Weinberg|journal = Cell|volume = 137|issue = 6|pages = 1032–1046|df = mdy-all|doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2009.03.047|pmid = 19524507|pmc = 2766609|date = June 12, 2009|last1 = Weinberg|first1 = Robert A.|last2 = Richardson|first2 = Andrea L.|last3 = Brock|first3 = Jane E.|last4 = Wang|first4 = Zhigang C.|last5 = Szász|first5 = Attila M.|last6 = Calogrias|first6 = Diana|last7 = Benaich|first7 = Nathan|last8 = Reinhardt|first8 = Ferenc|last9 = Valastyan|first9 = Scott}}{{Retracted|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2015.03.047|pmid=25879117|http://retractionwatch.com/the-retraction-watch-leaderboard/top-10-most-highly-cited-retracted-papers/ ''Retraction Watch''|http://retractionwatch.com/2015/04/03/other-shoe-drops-for-mit-cancer-researcher-robert-weinberg-as-cell-retraction-appears/ ''Retraction Watch''|intentional=yes}}</ref> This is out of over 450 publications since 1963.

The reasons given for the retraction of one paper (DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2009.03.04) include: "Falsification/Fabrication of Data" and "Manipulation of Results".
